video_title: MacroVoices #551 Michael Every: Decoding The Global Geopolitical Puzzle
gist: Rabobank's Michael Every argues the oil sell-off is unjustified 'hope': both the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars are closer to escalation than peace, a genuine diesel crisis is possible after Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, and energy is heading from one integrated global market toward US-led closed-loop blocs and statecraft (diesel export curbs, the new permanent Greenland deal, stablecoin lending via the DFC). The market desk adds a USO bull call spread, flags the 10-year Treasury above 5% (highest since 2007) with ~70% odds of an October Fed hike, a DXY breakout above 101, very narrow equity breadth, cheap 3-month VIX, and a crowded yen long.

insights.claim: Michael Every argues the latest drop in oil is driven largely by hope that is not justified by reality, since Yanbu, Riyadh, Aramco and the already-hit East-West pipeline can be attacked again and again.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Crude sell-offs on peace headlines may be opportunities to re-establish upside exposure rather than signals that the geopolitical premium is gone.
insights.quote: unless you have discrete and distinct knowledge of when these wars will end, you are just hoping

insights.claim: Every's framework: once the US economic blockade on Iran started working, Iran's incentive was to escalate militarily elsewhere (directly or via proxies like the Houthis in the Red Sea), which pushed Brent up to about $110 for a while.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Tighter economic pressure on Iran raises, not lowers, the odds of attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping lanes.

insights.claim: Every's base case is a US escalation against Iran once the US election is out of the way regardless of who wins, most likely with Israel and a GCC coalition 'to try and really finish the job', and possibly earlier if Iran escalates first.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Oil and rates hedges should extend beyond the US election date; the post-election period is the highlighted escalation window, not a peace window.
insights.quote: That is our base case that you will see escalation once the election's out of the way.

insights.claim: Every dismisses the Trump administration's claim that Iran will sign a peace deal right after the US election, saying the two sides' starting and finishing positions remain irreconcilable and the blockade is working well for the US.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Discount official peace-deal timelines when pricing the oil risk premium.

insights.claim: Iran, Putin and other Trump adversaries have a strong incentive to keep oil prices elevated through the US election to hurt Republicans; Every agrees this dynamic must be kept in mind at all times.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host), agreed by Michael Every
insights.so_what: Adversaries' electoral incentives skew near-term energy supply risk to the upside into the election.

insights.claim: Asked whether Trump could launch a 'Hail Mary' military escalation before the election to claim he finished the war, Every would not rule it out and said serious people are seriously discussing it.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: A pre-election escalation spike is a live tail; long-dated oil upside optionality is cheap insurance against it.
insights.quote: serious people who take this matter seriously are having serious discussions about the serious likelihood of that happening

insights.claim: Every's energy-as-strategic-asset framework: the Americas and the Middle East together are the only energy/refining holdings that matter globally; if the US defeats Iran it controls both, and if it cannot, keeping the Middle East destabilized still leaves the Americas bloc with strong relative leverage over China and others.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: The US may tolerate higher energy prices and prolonged Gulf instability as a strategic win, so do not assume political pain forces a quick de-escalation.

insights.claim: Every calls Venezuela a fantastic success for the US in geopolitical and oil terms, the template Trump hoped to replicate in Iran.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Western Hemisphere oil supply is increasingly aligned with US strategic control.

themes.theme: Russian refinery strikes and diesel crisis risk

insights.claim: Days after Trump publicly warned Zelensky not to hit Russian refineries because the world needs diesel, Ukraine struck Russian diesel refining, reportedly taking out around 40% of Russia's diesel refining capacity (a figure the host said he had not verified).
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: A large chunk of global diesel supply may be offline, tightening middle distillates independent of crude.

insights.claim: Every says record diesel prices are now appearing not just in the US but worldwide, with serious signs of political stress, economic stress and even social unrest in some countries, and it will get worse the longer it lasts.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Diesel cracks and distillate-heavy economies (agriculture, logistics) are the pressure points; watch for social unrest in import-dependent countries.

insights.claim: Rabobank's energy strategist is deeply concerned that a genuine, serious diesel crisis is possible, given low inventories, the West having closed refineries for years without building new ones, and Middle East disruption that could come roaring back alongside the damage to Russia.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Refining capacity, not crude, may be the binding constraint; refiners and distillate spreads carry the upside.

insights.claim: Anas Alhajji, who previously argued $200 oil would appear only in local markets and not benchmarks, is now warning that diesel is the crisis after the Russian refinery strikes.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend (host)
insights.so_what: When a habitually non-alarmist energy analyst flags diesel, the product-market signal deserves weight over headline crude.

insights.claim: Every's second-order read of the refinery strikes: if the US curbed diesel exports, Europe would suffer most and would be forced to rein in Ukraine and push toward a settlement; he also cites oil-trader whispers that refined products are still arbitraged from Europe to Russia.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Diesel supply leverage could become the channel through which a Russia-Ukraine settlement is forced; don't trade only the first-order Trump headline.
insights.quote: don't always fall for the first order Trump related headline

insights.claim: Every notes that apart from Trump nobody is angry with Zelensky for the refinery strikes, even as Europe suffers from the diesel crisis, and the mainstream narrative blames Trump in a unidirectional way; he suspects there is more to the strikes than seeking attention.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Mainstream narrative framing may be a poor guide to actual policy intentions; discount consensus explanations.

insights.claim: Every judges both the Russia-Ukraine and Middle East wars to be far closer to escalation than to peace, and increasingly to be conflating into what is effectively the same war fought by different people.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Correlated escalation risk across two energy-producing regions argues against positioning for peace-driven energy price declines.
insights.quote: we're far closer to escalation than we are to peace in our time

themes.theme: Energy blocs, export curbs and statecraft

insights.claim: Every says rates and FX traders now effectively have to be oil traders to forecast bond yields, and oil traders in turn must understand who wins wars and who is bluffing; central bank reaction functions (Fed, ECB, Bank of England) are all reactions to geopolitics.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Rate and FX views should be conditioned on geopolitical/energy scenarios rather than just GDP and CPI data.
insights.quote: if you're an interest rate trader or an FX trader at the moment, you have to be an oil trader

insights.claim: Neither Every nor the oil people he knows believe a US diesel export ban would keep US diesel prices low while global prices stay high, which the administration apparently believes.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Under an integrated global market, an export ban would fail to insulate US prices, but Every warns that assumption itself may be breaking.

insights.claim: Every's contrarian hypothesis: with tariffs, protectionism and decoupling spreading, the still fully integrated 'one world' energy market is not viable, and the US will move toward a closed-loop North American energy bloc ('NAPHTA') with allies sharing its China tariffs and defense umbrella, leaving the rest of the world to 'knock at the door and beg'.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Energy experts modeling a permanently integrated global market may be wrong; regional price dislocations (US vs rest-of-world product prices) could widen.

insights.claim: Every lists US statecraft tools for energy: using the Defense Production Act to direct refineries and order more diesel storage, floating storage on ships, and regional storage, treating energy as national security rather than a business sector.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: US refiners' economics could be shaped by government direction; policy risk to refiner margins and export volumes is rising.

insights.claim: Every expects any US diesel export restriction to be selective rather than binary, and says a blanket ban would burn geopolitical bridges and undermine America's energy-dominance export strategy.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Watch for targeted, country-specific export curbs rather than a blanket ban.

insights.claim: Every floats Brazil as a possible target for US diesel export cuts if its presidential election goes to Lula and Lula tilts toward China and Russia, while a Bolsonaro-direction win would leave only Canada and Nicaragua outside the 'Donroe doctrine'.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Brazil's election outcome could determine its access to US refined products, relevant to Brazilian agriculture and assets.

insights.claim: The Netherlands, which re-exports US diesel into the rest of Europe, is the other big market that could be cut off as leverage in US-Europe disputes.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: European diesel supply is exposed to US policy decisions, amplifying European energy risk.

insights.claim: America did not export crude between 1975 and 2015, a precedent Every notes most people have forgotten when dismissing export restrictions.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: US energy export restrictions have long precedent and should not be dismissed as unthinkable.

insights.claim: The new US-Denmark-Greenland security agreement is permanent, survives a Greenland independence vote, lets the US expand bases with Denmark informed but without a veto, and gives the US veto rights over others investing in Greenland's minerals and potential oil.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: The US has secured first dibs on Greenland's resources and blocked Chinese/Russian access; Arctic minerals exposure now runs through US approval.
insights.quote: It's also now permanent. It's forever.

insights.claim: Every argues the Greenland deal gave the US nearly everything it wanted short of Denmark paying for the bases, while the media wrongly mocked it as Trump signing for what he already had; the European climb-down contradicts the earlier doom headlines.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: First-order headline panic over Trump's coercion has repeatedly resolved in US-favorable deals; fade the doom narrative.

insights.claim: Greenland matters strategically because ICBMs aimed at the US would come over the North Pole, and together with Iceland (which just voted not to join the EU) it corks the Arctic shipping passage that Russia or China could increasingly use as waters warm.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Arctic chokepoint control and missile defense make Greenland a durable US priority, relevant to defense and Arctic resource plays.

insights.claim: Every says he heard the Greenland outcome as a rumor five or six weeks before it was announced, illustrating that markets reading only Bloomberg screens and mainstream headlines get blindsided.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Geopolitical second- and third-order analysis, not headline-following, is where the edge is.

insights.claim: Every's read on China: it wins from the peaceful status quo, has armored its economy with stockpiles and redundancies so it cannot be easily coerced, and wants both wars to stop but does not want Russia or Iran to lose.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: China is unlikely to aggressively back either Russia or Iran, but will keep building redundancies; don't expect China to broker a quick end.

insights.claim: Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, China reportedly proposed extending the trade truce (lower tariffs, rare earths flowing) to the end of Trump's term, but the US would only consider 3 to 6 months, which Every reads as the US believing it will hold a new card within that window.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: A short truce extension implies a potential US-China trade flashpoint in 3-6 months; rare-earth and tariff-sensitive assets face renewed risk.

insights.claim: Every sees a generalized trend toward tariffs, protectionism, decoupling and fragmentation continuing despite the upcoming Trump summit, with Europe increasingly talking about a trade war with China to protect its industry.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Fragmentation is the structural backdrop; summit optics should not be mistaken for a reversal.

insights.claim: The Clarity Act failed and is stalled in Congress, removing the 'adrenaline shot' a clear legal framework (including rules on interest versus rewards) would have given dollar stablecoins.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: The legislative catalyst for dollar stablecoin growth is delayed.

insights.claim: Per reporting by Izabella Kaminska, the Development Finance Corporation has a new unit, SWORD, that makes strategic lending or 'money drops' worldwide to strengthen supply chains and US national security, and it will do so in stablecoins.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Dollar stablecoins are being operationalized as a geopolitical tool, supporting long-run stablecoin demand irrespective of Congress.

insights.claim: Every concludes the US is deadly serious about stablecoin statecraft and that Congress failing to pass the Clarity Act will not stop it; it will happen via more surreptitious, cloak-and-dagger channels than the traditional banking system.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Legislative setbacks are a weak signal for dollar-stablecoin adoption; watch executive-branch agencies instead.
insights.quote: just because Congress doesn't approve it doesn't mean it isn't going to happen

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna's trade: a USO bull call spread expiring January 15, 2027 (about 113 days), buying the $150 call for about $15.50 and selling the $180 call for about $7.25, an $8.25 debit on a $30-wide spread for close to 3:1 reward/risk, with USO referenced at $148.30 and $180 roughly equal to crude near $120.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Defined-risk way to position for renewed crude strength while oil volatility sits near the low end of its recent range.

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield broke decisively above 5% to around 5.10%, the highest since 2007, even as crude dropped almost $10 from its highs; the 30-year is above 5.40% and the 10-year real yield is around 2.7%.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Yields decoupling from oil means the bond sell-off has its own drivers; rising hurdle rates pressure equity valuations, mortgages and financial conditions.

insights.claim: Fed funds futures price close to 70% odds of a rate hike in October and over 50% odds of back-to-back hikes in October and December.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Markets are pricing a hiking cycle; the speed of yield rises is the key variable for every other asset and may prompt stabilization attempts.

insights.claim: S&P 500 breadth is extremely narrow: only 28% of stocks are above their 50-day moving average, the equal-weight index is making lower lows, the Russell 2000 shows sell signals and financials are breaking down, while about five mega-cap AI names carry the index.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Cap-weighted strength masks broad weakness; a mega-cap stumble could trigger a correction.

insights.claim: Ceresna sees the S&P 500 capable of reaching 8,000-8,200 if it breaks to 52-week highs and breadth widens, but if the 10-year presses toward 5.25%-5.50% it could be the catalyst for a roughly 10% correction into the midterms.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Use the 10-year yield path as the switch between a breakout scenario and a correction scenario.

insights.claim: The 30-day VIX is around 15 and the 3-month VIX, which spans the election, jobs data and the October earnings cycle, is at its year lows, making portfolio insurance about as cheap as it has been all year.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Stay long but buy cheap downside protection through year-end.
insights.quote: the cost of insuring is about as cheap as it's been all year

insights.claim: The dollar index broke above 101 out of an 18-month 97-100 range even though short-term rates are rising everywhere so rate differentials are not diverging, which Ceresna reads as a possible sign of dollar funding stress; the euro, the largest DXY component, is most vulnerable, with a possible move to 1.08-1.10.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A DXY break to 52-week highs alongside rates stress would be an immediate disruptor for risk assets.

insights.claim: Ceresna says crude's pullback, after a run from about $80 to about $105 in two weeks, is a headline-driven pause at a 50% retracement and the 50-day moving average; with depleted inventories, $110-$120 oil remains on the table, and a breakout off the $90 level is the key thing to watch.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A renewed oil spike would further disrupt rates and make bond-market stabilization harder, hurting risk assets.

insights.claim: Gold's early-August breakout came when Treasury Secretary Bessent announced intervention in the long end of the curve, but post-Jackson Hole higher real yields and a stronger dollar have left gold on a knife's edge below its 50-day moving average, risking a false start that pushes the next bull leg to late Q4 or Q1.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Gold longs need dollar and rates stabilization; a new DXY high with gold below the 50-day would confirm a failed breakout.

insights.claim: Copper positioning is crowded long near the 100th percentile, yet a tariff-driven 7% correction was bought immediately and copper is back at 52-week highs, so Ceresna respects the bull trend while dips keep getting bought.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Crowding alone is not a sell signal; trend-follow copper until dip-buying fails.

insights.claim: Uranium spot (U3O8) stays near 90 and the physical uranium trust is stable, but uranium equities are tired with rallies fading; a break below 40 on URA would keep a distribution cycle in play with possible downside to 35.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Uranium equities are diverging from the commodity; wait for a base before buying the miners.

insights.claim: Large speculators swung from roughly 92,000 contracts net short to more than 120,000 net long Japanese yen in two weeks (about 110,000 contracts in one week, more than full-year repositioning in 2022-23), reaching the 1-year 100th percentile as of September 15, before the yen fell about 200 pips on the dollar rally.
insights.speaker: Market desk co-host and Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A crowded yen long facing a dollar funding squeeze could be forced out; watch for a positioning washout.
